title: Two Sisters, One Piano Bench, and 55 Years of Musical Magic
summary: What if you and your sibling shared a piano bench for over 55 years? That's the story of Katia and Marielle Labèque, two French sisters who are still making music together. Their new album, called 55, has 55 tracks—one for each year they've been recording. But this isn't just a look back. Almost half the songs are brand new! And here's the cool part: many are by women composers, like the mysterious Ethiopian nun Emahoy Tsegué-Maryam Guèbrou. The sisters admit they didn't pay enough attention to women composers before. Now they're fixing that. Some tracks are wild, like a two-piano version of Stravinsky's Rite of Spring that sounds like a beast roaring out of the piano. Others are gentle, like a tiny waltz by Marie Jaëll, a forgotten French composer who was friends with Liszt. Sometimes the sisters play on two separate pianos, and sometimes they squeeze onto one bench for four-handed pieces. Either way, they finish each other's musical sentences with perfect timing and fearless energy. It all started in 1969 when a famous composer heard them practice and wanted to record with just one sister. They said no—they were sticking together. That decision launched a lifetime of music that still surprises us today.
why_it_matters: This story shows that working together with a sibling or friend can create incredible things that last a lifetime, and that even small choices (like sharing a piano bench) can lead to a lifetime of joy and surprises.

background_read: Katia and Marielle Labèque are a world-famous piano duo from France who started playing together when they were very young.
Emahoy Tsegué-Maryam Guèbrou (an Ethiopian nun and composer) wrote gentle, beautiful piano pieces that were recorded long ago and only became widely known much later.
Igor Stravinsky was a Russian composer whose music 'The Rite of Spring' was so wild and new that it caused a riot at its first performance.
Article_Structure: WHO: Katia and Marielle Labèque, two French sisters who have played the piano together for over 55 years.
WHAT: They released a new album called '55' with 55 tracks, including many by women composers, two-piano versions, and waltzes.
WHERE: In recording studios and on concert stages, starting from their early practice room to performances around the world.
WHY: To celebrate their long career, correct earlier oversights by featuring more music from women, and share their fearless musical energy.

perspectives.description: The sisters prove that sticking together and supporting each other can result in a magical career that spans decades. Their perfect timing and fearless energy inspire anyone who wants to make something special with a partner.

By admitting they didn't pay enough attention to women composers before, the sisters show that it's okay to realize a mistake and fix it. This teaches us to keep learning and make sure many different voices are heard.
The album is not just a look back; it is full of brand-new pieces. The mix of wild, roaring two-piano performances and gentle waltzes makes the music exciting for both old fans and new listeners.
